question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=x+4y$ and $f_y(x,y)=3x-y$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=2x$ and $f_y(x,y)=0$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=2x+\cos{x}\cos{y}$ and $f_y(x,y)=e^y-\sin{x}\sin{y}$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (x+4y) = 4 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (3x-y) = 3. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) \neq f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair cannot represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (2x) = 0 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (0) = 0. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( 2x+\cos{x}\cos{y} \big) \\[3pt] &= 0 + \cos{x} \cdot (-\sin{y} ) \\[3pt] &= -\cos{x}\sin{y}, \\[7pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( e^y-\sin{x}\sin{y} \big) \\[3pt] &= 0 - \sin{y} \cdot \cos{x} \\[3pt] &=-\cos{x}\sin{y}. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'II and III only'.

example.title: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives

question.text: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate $f_{yxx}\left(1,1\right)$ if $f_{xy}(x,y)=ye^{xy}\left(2+xy\right).$
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

\begin{align*} f_{yxx}(x,y) & = f_{xyx}(x,y) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_{xy}(x,y) \big) \\[3pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( ye^{xy}\left(2+xy\right) \big) \\[3pt] &= y^2e^{xy}\left(2+xy\right) + y^2e^{xy} \\[3pt] &=y^2e^{xy}\left(3+xy\right). \\[7pt] \end{align*}

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $\left(1,1\right)\mathbin{:}$

\[ f_{yxx}\left(1,1\right) = (1)^2e^{1\cdot 1}\left(3+(1)(1)\right) = 4e \\[7pt] \]

example.title: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

question.text:
Suppose that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U.$ Which of the following pairs could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y)?$

  1. $f_x(x,y)=x^2-2y$ and $f_y(x,y)=y^2-2x$
  2. $f_x(x,y)=\sqrt{\dfrac{y}{x}}+3x^2y$ and $f_y(x,y)=\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{y}}+x^3$
  3. $f_x(x,y)=e^{x+1}\sin{(x-1)}$ and $f_y(x,y)=e^{\sqrt{y}}$
question.explanation:
Since the function and its first and second-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal, that is, $f_{xy}(x,y)=f_{yx}(x,y).$ Let's check if this condition is true for each of our pairs of first-order partial derivatives.

  • For the first pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} (x^2-2y) = -2 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} (y^2-2x) = -2. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the first pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the second pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \left( \sqrt{\dfrac{y}{x}}+3x^2y \right)= \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{yx}} + 3x^2 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \left(\sqrt{\dfrac{x}{y}}+x^3 \right)=\dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{xy}}+3x^2. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y) = f_{yx}(x,y)$, the second pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

  • For the third pair, we have \begin{align*} f_{xy}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \big( e^{x+1}\sin{(x-1)}\big)= 0 \\[3pt] f_{yx}(x,y) &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big(e^{\sqrt{y}} \big)=0. \end{align*} As $f_{xy}(x,y)= f_{yx}(x,y)$, the third pair could represent the first-order partial derivatives of $f(x,y).$

Therefore, the correct answer is 'I, II and III'.

example.title: Identifying Possible Pairs of First-Order Partial Derivatives

question.text: Given that the function $f(x,y)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ evaluate $f_{yxy}(1,2)$ if $f_{yy}(x,y)=x^2y^3\sin(2x-y).$
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal. Hence, we have

\begin{align*} f_{yxy}(x,y) & = f_{yyx}(x,y) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( f_{yy}(x,y) \big) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \big( x^2y^3\sin(2x-y) \big) \\[5pt] &= y^3 \left( 2x \cdot \sin(2x-y) + x^2 \cdot \cos(2x-y) \cdot 2 \right) \\[5pt] &= 2xy^3 ( \sin(2x-y) + x\cos(2x-y)) . \end{align*}

Now, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,2)\mathbin{:}$

\[ f_{xyx}(1,2) = 2\cdot 1 \cdot 2^3 \cdot ( \sin(2\cdot 1- 2) + 1\cdot \cos(2\cdot 1- 2)) = 16. \]

example.title: Evaluating Expressions of Partial Derivatives at a Point

question.text:
Suppose that a function $f(x,y,z)$ and all of its higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ and that

\[ \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} = \dfrac{xe^{yz}}{x+y}, \qquad \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial z} = -\dfrac{ze^{yz}}{x+y}. \]

Evaluate the following expression at the point $(1,1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\[ \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial y\partial x\partial y}+ \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial z \partial x \partial z} \]
question.explanation:
As the higher-order partial derivatives are continuous on an open set $U,$ the mixed partial derivatives must be equal.

Hence, we have

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial y\partial x\partial y} &= \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial x \partial y^2} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}\left( \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial y^2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}\left( \dfrac{xe^{yz}}{x+y} \right) \\[5pt] &= e^{yz} \cdot \left( \dfrac{1\cdot (x+y) - x\cdot 1}{(x+y)^2} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{ye^{yz}}{(x+y)^2} . \end{align*}

In addition, we have \begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial z \partial x \partial z} &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial z} \left( \dfrac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x\partial z} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{\partial }{\partial z} \left( -\dfrac{ze^{yz}}{x+y} \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{1}{x+y} \cdot (e^{yz}+yze^{yz}) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{e^{yz}(1+yz)}{x+y}. \end{align*}

Now, we evaluate both partial derivatives at the point $(1,1,0)\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial x\partial y\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,1,0)} &= \dfrac{1\cdot e^{1\cdot 0}}{(1+1)^2} = \dfrac{1}{4} \\[7pt] \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial z \partial x \partial z} \Bigg|_{(1,1,0)} &= -\dfrac{e^{1\cdot 0}(1+1\cdot 0)}{1+1} =- \dfrac{1}{2} \end{align*}

Finally, we get

\begin{align*} \dfrac{\partial^3 f}{\partial x\partial y\partial x} \Bigg|_{(1,1,0)} + \dfrac{\partial^3 f }{\partial z \partial x \partial z} \Bigg|_{(1,1,0)} &= \dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{2} =- \dfrac{1}{4}. \end{align*}
